body.p: This study presents a potentially important strategy for improving whole-tumor-cell vaccines by combining senescent tumor cells with COX-2 inhibition and hydrogel-based delivery. The evidence supporting enhanced antitumor immune responses is convincing, based on mechanistic experiments and therapeutic studies across multiple mouse tumor models. However, the specific contribution of cDC1s, the identity of the relevant tumor antigens, and the long-term safety of administering live senescent cells require future investigation.
Summary

The authors developed a whole-tumor-cell vaccination strategy using senescent tumor cells (STCs) encapsulated within a chitosan hydrogel containing liposomal celecoxib, a COX2 inhibitor. This approach aims to take advantage of the immunogenic properties of senescent tumor cells while limiting the immunosuppressive effects of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), a component of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).

The authors show that inhibiting PGE2 production enhances natural killer (NK) cell activation, promotes dendritic cell (DC) recruitment and maturation, and stimulates antitumor T-cell responses. The therapeutic efficacy of this platform is demonstrated in several mouse tumor models, including subcutaneous melanoma, intracranial melanoma, and orthotopic pancreatic cancer.
Strengths
(1) Vaccine design

A major strength of this study is its approach to exploiting the immunogenic properties of senescent tumor cells while addressing the immunosuppressive effects of the SASP. By combining STCs with localized COX2 inhibition, the authors reduce PGE2-mediated immune suppression while maintaining the secretion of immunostimulatory factors. The hydrogel-based delivery system also prolongs local cell retention, potentially allowing more sustained immune stimulation.
(2) Mechanistic evidence supporting COX2/PGE2 inhibition

The study provides convincing mechanistic evidence supporting the role of COX2/PGE2 inhibition in restoring NK cell-DC interactions. The authors demonstrate enhanced NK cell activation, increased secretion of CCL5 and XCL1, improved DC recruitment, and increased activation of cytotoxic T cells.

Experiments using an alternative COX2 inhibitor, meloxicam, together with exogenous PGE2 rescue, further support the involvement of this pathway in regulating DC recruitment. These findings help distinguish the effects of COX2/PGE2 inhibition from those potentially specific to celecoxib.
(3) Antigen-dependent vaccine efficacy

The study also examines whether the therapeutic effects depend on senescence-specific antigens or tumor antigens shared between senescent and proliferating cancer cells. Experiments comparing antigen-matched and mismatched senescent tumor cell vaccines demonstrate greater therapeutic efficacy when the vaccine and tumor share the same cellular origin.

These findings support an antigen-dependent component of the therapeutic response and suggest that the vaccine can elicit immunity against antigens shared between senescent and proliferating tumor cells. This is relevant because the intended therapeutic targets are primarily non-senescent tumor cells.
(4) Efficacy across multiple tumor models

The therapeutic potential of the vaccine is evaluated across several tumor models. The authors demonstrate significant tumor growth inhibition in subcutaneous melanoma, prolonged survival in an intracranial melanoma model, and reduced tumor burden in an orthotopic pancreatic cancer model. The activity observed across these different settings suggests that the approach may have applications beyond a single tumor type.
(5) Hydrogel degradation and local safety

The study includes an evaluation of hydrogel degradation and local tissue responses. The hydrogel progressively degrades and is no longer detectable by approximately 28 days, with no apparent tissue damage or abnormal inflammatory infiltration at the injection site during this period. These observations provide useful information regarding the local biocompatibility of the formulation.
Weaknesses and Opportunities for Future Investigation
(1) Role of cDC1 in therapeutic efficacy

Although the study demonstrates increased DC recruitment and activation, the requirement for conventional type 1 dendritic cells (cDC1s) in mediating the observed antitumor effects has not been directly established. Experiments using cDC1-deficient mice or selective depletion approaches would help determine whether this population is essential for vaccine-induced T-cell responses and tumor control. The current findings support the involvement of cDC1s but do not establish their necessity.
(2) Long-term safety and SASP heterogeneity

The hydrogel degradation and histological studies provide evidence of local biocompatibility over the period examined. However, the longer-term consequences of administering metabolically active senescent tumor cells remain uncertain. Hydrogel degradation does not necessarily establish complete clearance of the encapsulated cells, and the SASP contains factors with potentially opposing effects on inflammation and tumor progression.

Although celecoxib reduces PGE2 without significantly altering the measured levels of IL-6 and TNF-α, a more comprehensive assessment of SASP composition and longer-term systemic responses would be useful, particularly given the heterogeneity of senescence across tumor types and induction conditions.
(3) Antigen specificity

The comparison between matched and mismatched vaccines provides evidence that tumor-associated antigens contribute to therapeutic efficacy. However, the specific antigens recognized by vaccine-induced T cells remain undefined. Direct measurements of antigen-specific T-cell responses would help distinguish the contributions of adaptive antigen recognition and innate immune activation to the observed therapeutic effects.
Overall Evaluation

This study presents an approach to improving whole-tumor-cell vaccines by combining senescent tumor cells with COX2 inhibition and hydrogel-based delivery. The mechanistic experiments and therapeutic studies provide convincing evidence that this formulation enhances antitumor immune responses, with activity demonstrated across several mouse tumor models. Although the specific requirement for cDC1s, the identity of the relevant tumor antigens, and the longer-term safety of live senescent cells remain to be established, the findings provide a useful foundation for further development of senescent tumor cell-based cancer vaccines.
Summary:

Wang et al. examined an engineered senescent tumor cell-based live vaccine, in which senescent tumor cells are co-encapsulated with liposomal celecoxib in a chitosan hydrogel. The authors propose that prolonged persistence of senescent cells, combined with COX2/PGE2 inhibition, restores natural killer cell and dendritic cell crosstalk, enhances type 1 conventional dendritic cell recruitment, and drives robust CD8+ T-cell-mediated anti-tumor immunity. The study is nicely executed and clearly presented, with extensive in vitro and in vivo validation across multiple tumor models, including melanoma brain metastases and orthotopic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. The revision adds four new experiments and substantially expands the discussion, and addresses most of the concerns raised previously.

In the revised version, the authors have directly tested whether the vaccine works through senescence-specific antigens or through antigens shared with the parental tumor. Using matched and antigen-mismatched senescent cell vaccines in mice bearing the same tumor, they find that the matched vaccine is considerably more effective, and they have accordingly removed their earlier speculation about senescence-specific neoantigens from the discussion. This is a well-designed comparison, and the authors willingness to revise their interpretation in light of the new data is a strength of the revision. As presented, the statement that these data demonstrate the point is stronger than the evidence supports. The comparison between the two vaccine arms, which is the contrast on which the conclusion depends, is also not shown statistically in the figure.

The authors have likewise strengthened the case that the immunological effects reflect prostaglandin E2 suppression rather than properties peculiar to celecoxib, by showing a comparable effect with a second inhibitor and reversal by added prostaglandin E2. The logic of this experiment is sound and the rescue arm is the appropriate control. However, the result is shown only as representative images, without cell counts, sample sizes, or statistical analysis, whereas the equivalent experiment in the original submission was quantified. In its present form, readers cannot judge the magnitude or reliability of the effect.

On the question of eventual clearance of the senescent cells, the authors now provide a time course showing that the hydrogel degrades fully within four weeks, with no histological evidence of tissue damage. This is a useful addition. It should be noted, however, that this experiment documents the fate of the delivery matrix rather than of the cells themselves, so the inference that exposure of the local tissue to senescent cells and their secretory products is bounded at approximately four weeks does not strictly follow from it. The authors already report imaging of labelled senescent cells elsewhere in the manuscript, and extending that readout across the same time course would address the question directly. Degradation is also assessed only by gross photographs, and the absence of immune infiltration is based on histology without quantification.

The authors have appropriately acknowledged that the requirement for type 1 conventional dendritic cells was not tested, explaining that the relevant genetic models were unavailable. This is a reasonable position, and the limitation is candidly stated. Readers should therefore understand the proposed innate-to-adaptive mechanism as correlative, some of the surrounding language in the discussion still implies a causal chain that has not been established. The remaining points raised previously, concerning senescence heterogeneity, terminology, and translational considerations, have been addressed satisfactorily through new discussion sections.
Strengths:
(1) Strong conceptual framework combining senescence biology and biomaterials.
(2) Impressive breadth of in vivo models, including brain metastasis and orthotopic pancreatic cancer.
(3) Clear immunological readouts.
(4) A well-controlled new experiment distinguishing shared from senescence-specific tumor antigens, with the interpretation revised accordingly.
Evidence that the effect reflects prostaglandin E2 suppression rather than a single compound.
Weaknesses:
(1) The requirement for type 1 conventional dendritic cells remains untested, so the proposed mechanism is correlative.
(2) Several new supporting datasets are presented without quantification, sample sizes, or statistical analysis.
(3) Clearance of the senescent cells themselves is inferred from degradation of the delivery matrix rather than measured directly.
The following is the authors’ response to the original reviews.

disp-quote.p: (1) While the authors successfully inhibit PGE2, the SASP is a complex cocktail of factors. The discussion regarding the long-term presence of these "live" senescent cells is somewhat limited. Although the hydrogel retains cells locally, the potential for other chronic inflammatory factors to eventually promote tumorigenesis or tissue damage in the surrounding niche warrants careful consideration when translating this approach to patients and may require additional preclinical testing.

body.p: We have provided new experimental data to address this concern. Specifically, we performed a serial in vivo study in which the hydrogel vaccine was injected subcutaneously, and the injection site was harvested on days 1, 3, 7, 14, 21, and 28 for gross observation of gel degradation and H&E histological examination (Figure S11).

The results showed that the hydrogel began to degrade around day 3, degraded progressively thereafter, and was completely degraded by day 28 (Figure S11A). Importantly, H&E staining revealed no abnormal immune-cell infiltration or tissue damage in the surrounding skin at any time point, indicating local biosafety throughout the entire residence window (Figure S11B). Together with our existing biosafety data, these results indicate that the exposure of the local niche to live STCs and their secretome is temporally bounded (~4 weeks) rather than indefinite, which substantially limits the risk of chronic inflammation or pro-tumorigenic tissue remodeling.

disp-quote.p: (2) The study posits that STCs serve as an antigen reservoir. However, the manuscript would benefit from a clearer distinction between whether the immune system is recognizing senescence-specific neoantigens or simply shared tumor antigens that are being presented more effectively due to the adjuvant effect. The authors briefly touch upon neoantigens in the discussion, but the experimental data primarily measure general anti-tumor responses.

body.p: The detailed reply is provided in the R1-1 response.

disp-quote.p: (R1-1) Clarification of Antigen Source: The discussion mentions that senescence generates neoantigens. It would be beneficial to include data or an expanded discussion comparing the antigenic profile of the STCs versus the parental tumor cells. Does the vaccine protect against non-senescent tumor rechallenge primarily because of shared antigens, or are the T-cells specifically targeting senescence markers.

body.p: To address this issue, we carried out a new therapeutic experiment, which we designed to functionally dissect the relative contribution of senescence-specific neoantigens versus shared tumor antigens (Figure S9). We established subcutaneous LLC tumor-bearing mice and compared three treatment groups on day 11: (i) PBS control; (ii) matched vaccine (LLC-CLX-Lipo@Gel: senescent LLC cell vaccine); and (iii) mismatched vaccine (B16F10-CLX-Lipo@Gel: senescent B16F10 cell vaccine). The matched LLC-CLX-Lipo@Gel achieved a tumor inhibition rate of approximately 90%, whereas the mismatched B16F10-CLX-Lipo@Gel inhibited tumor growth by only 40% compared to PBS. These findings indicate that the antitumor immunity elicited by the vaccine primarily targets tumor antigens shared between senescent cells and their parental tumor cells. The residual efficacy of the mismatched vaccine (~40%) likely reflects the SASP-driven innate components (e.g., NK-cell activation and recruitment).

disp-quote.p: (R1-2) Comparison to Standard Lysates: In Figure 2, the authors compare STCs to "Died STCs" (cells subjected to freeze/thaw, essentially lysates at this point). While STCs performed better, it would be helpful to explicitly discuss why the live metabolic state is crucial. Is it solely the continuous secretion of chemokines (SASP) that makes the difference? A brief clarification on the duration of SASP secretion within the hydrogel in vivo would strengthen this claim.

body.p: We have now addressed this issue in the revised Discussion. The live metabolic state of STCs may contribute through two complementary mechanisms:

- Sustained adjuvant/secretory function: The SASP is an actively regulated, translationally controlled secretory program. Live STCs therefore continually replenish chemokines and cytokines and provide ongoing paracrine stimulation to immature immune cells within the gel depot, whereas a freeze/thaw lysate delivers only a single, finite bolus of pre-formed mediators and DAMPs. A similar advantage was also observed in a killed but metabolically active bacterial vaccine that highly elicits effector T-cell responses and benefits from the potency of live vaccines and the safety of non-proliferation (Brockstedt et al., 2005).

- Prolonged in situ antigen release: Sustained release from an in-situ depot outperforms bolus delivery (Kim et al., 2015). In our system, live STCs persist within the gel and release antigen under continuing innate activation, consistent with the observation that senescent cancer cell vaccines outperform immunogenic-cell-death vaccines (Marin et al., 2023a) and that antigen bursts from dying cells are insufficient on their own (Liu et al., 2023). Regarding the duration, our new degradation study shows the hydrogel matrix begins degrading at ~day 3 and is fully degraded by day 28 (Figure S11A), defining the upper bound of the in vivo secretory phase at approximately 4 weeks.

disp-quote.p: (R1-3) Hydrogel Degradation: More context or data regarding the degradation rate of the chitosan hydrogel in vivo. Knowing the physical integrity of the gel over this period is important for understanding the release kinetics of the liposomal celecoxib.

body.p: We have performed this experiment and provided the results (Figure S11A). Subcutaneous injection sites were monitored on days 1, 3, 7, 14, 21, and 28. The hydrogel began degrading around day 3 and was completely degraded by day 28, with no inflammatory cell infiltration detected in the adjacent skin at any time point (Figure S11B). This degradation timeline aligns with the intended release kinetics for early immune-priming and subsequent safe clearance. The result shows the physical disintegration kinetics of hydrogel matrix, suggesting the upper bound of the drug release at approximately 4 weeks.

disp-quote.p: (R1-4) Minor Point – SASP Components: The study focuses heavily on PGE2. It would be informative to check if Celecoxib treatment alters the secretion of other key SASP factors (e.g., IL-6, TGF-β) beyond just PGE2, to ensure the "good" chemokines are indeed unaffected.

body.p: We have performed an ELISA experiment to assess the anticancer SASP factors (IL-6 and TNF-α). The results revealed that celecoxib treatment did not significantly alter the secretion of IL-6 or TNF-α compared with vehicle-treated STCs (Figure S5). This indicates that celecoxib selectively suppresses the COX2/PGE2 arm without broadly suppressing the immunostimulatory SASP.

disp-quote.p: (1) The authors emphasize the expansion and activation of cDC1 as a key mechanism linking innate and adaptive immunity, yet it does not directly test whether cDC1 is required for the observed CD8+ T-cell responses and tumor control.

The authors should perform experiments using Batf3-deficient mice or any other cDC1-depletion strategies to provide important mechanistic validation. If such experiments are not feasible, this limitation should be more clearly acknowledged and discussed.

body.p: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's insightful and constructive comment regarding the causal validation of cDC1s in our therapeutic model. We fully agree that evaluating therapeutic outcomes in Batf3-deficient mice or via in vivo cDC1-depletion approaches represents the gold standard for establishing the indispensable role of this subset. Due to the current unavailability of the Batf3 knockout mouse strain and the experimental constraints, we were unable to conduct these specific animal experiments; we have thoroughly acknowledged this limitation in the revised discussion.

disp-quote.p: (2) The authors note that senescence may generate neoantigens distinct from those present in proliferating tumor cells, but the extent to which STC-induced immunity cross-reacts with non-senescent tumor cells is not fully addressed. While it is appreciated that tumor challenge experiments are included, the author should perform a more explicit analysis of antigenic overlap that would strengthen the translational relevance of the approach. For example, they can compare senescence induced by different stimuli or directly assess immune recognition of non-senescent tumor targets, which would help clarify whether the vaccine primarily exploits senescence-specific antigens or broadly shared tumor antigens.

body.p: We thank the Reviewer for this incisive comment. We first wish to correct the record. In the original Discussion we speculated that senescence generates neoantigens absent from parental tumor cells. Our new data do not support senescence-specific neoantigen dominance, and we have removed that statement from the revised Discussion. We address this raised issue in three parts.

(1) Cross-reactivity with non-senescent tumor cells is an operating principle of the study. In every efficacy experiment in the manuscript, the vaccine is composed of senescent cells whereas the target is an actively proliferating, non-senescent tumor of the same lineage. STC-elicited immunity therefore necessarily engages antigens expressed by proliferating tumor cells. What had remained untested was whether this cross-reactivity is antigen-repertoire-dependent, or merely the consequence of non-antigen-specific adjuvant activity. The new experiment addresses this question.

(2) In this new experiment (Figure S9), we compared a matched vaccine (senescent LLC) with an unmatched vaccine (senescent B16-F10) in mice bearing LLC tumors. Both cell lines are on the C57BL/6 background, and the unmatched arm isolates antigen-repertoire mismatch while excluding allogeneic rejection — the principal confounder of such comparisons. The two vaccines were prepared and administered using the same procedures, and the only variable that differs between the two arms is the antigen repertoire. Matched vaccination reduced tumor burden by ~90% versus PBS, whereas the unmatched vaccine achieved only 40%. The ~50-percentage-point difference suggests the antigen-dependent, lineage-restricted component of efficacy. It indicates that STC-elicited immunity recognizes non-senescent tumor cells, and that this cross-reactivity requires the tumor-antigen repertoire shared within the tumor lineage, rather than private senescence-specific antigens. From a translational standpoint this is favorable: the vaccine engages the proliferating tumor that constitutes the bulk of a patient's tumor burden, rather than the small senescent fraction.
(3) The residual activity of the mismatched vaccine is antigen-independent and is consistent with the SASP-driven innate arm that we document independently. Two lines of our own data bear on this:

- The cell-free components of the platform did not control tumor growth. In the prophylactic melanoma model, CS@Gel alone and CLX-Lipo alone — i.e., without STCs — did not restrain tumor growth (all non-STC groups exceeded 500 mm³ by day 14, versus 181 mm³ for the complete vaccine; Figure 7E–F). The residual activity of the mismatched vaccine therefore cannot be attributed to the hydrogel or to celecoxib.

- Senescent cells activate innate immunity directly. STCs, but not their non-senescent parental cells, increase DC maturation, CD8+ T-cell activation and NK-cell activation in vitro (Figure 1C–E), and elevate perforin and granzyme B in the culture supernatant (Figure 1F–G). Within the hydrogel, STCs+CLX-Lipo@Gel restored the NK–DC axis: NKG2D and NKp46 upregulation, increased NK proliferation and NK-mediated killing of tumor cells, and NK-derived CCL5/XCL1 secretion that recruits DCs (Figure 6B–K); in vivo, the same treatment increased circulating NK cells and activated NK cells (Figure 7G–I).

This is consistent with an established literature. Senescent tumor cells recruit, and are directly eliminated by, NK cells in a chemokine- and NKG2D-dependent manner (Iannello et al., 2013; Antonangeli et al., 2016, 2019), and NK-cell-derived CCL5 and XCL1 recruit cDC1 into tumors — a pathway that tumor-derived PGE₂ suppresses and that our CLX-Lipo component is designed to release (Böttcher et al., 2018). However, we are explicit about the limits of this interpretation: because this experiment did not include a cell-free arm under identical conditions, we cannot formally partition the residual activity, and a contribution from tumor antigens incidentally shared between two C57BL/6 tumor lines, cannot be excluded. We now state this limitation in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (3) Hydrogel encapsulation clearly extends STC persistence in vivo; however, the study provides limited information on the eventual clearance of these cells and the potential implications of prolonged SASP exposure. Given general concerns regarding chronic inflammation associated with senescent cells, additional discussion of long-term local and systemic responses would be helpful. If extended safety analyses are beyond the scope of the current study, the authors should acknowledge the limitation.

body.p: We have generated new data directly informing the clearance question. Serial observation on days 1, 3, 7, 14, 21, and 28 showed that the hydrogel was completely degraded by day 28 (Figure S11A). H&E staining of the injection-site skin showed no immune-cell infiltration or tissue pathology at any time point (Figure S11B). The results suggest long-term local biocompatibility of the hydrogel vaccine. Yet, the long-term systemic response remains further investigation.

disp-quote.p: (4) The immunological effects are attributed to COX2/PGE2 inhibition, but it remains unclear whether these effects are specific to celecoxib or could reflect formulation-dependent or off-target mechanisms. The authors may perform additional experiments employing an alternative COX2 inhibitor, genetic COX2 suppression, or PGE2 rescue, which could further support the specificity of the COX2/PGE2-dependent mechanism.

body.p: We have performed the suggested experiment using two of the proposed strategies: an alternative COX2 inhibitor (meloxicam, MLX) and exogenous PGE2 rescue. We utilized a transwell chemoattraction assay for BMDCs co-cultured with treated NK cells. Both celecoxib and meloxicam markedly enhanced NK-mediated BMDC migration compared to PBS or untreated STC groups. Crucially, the addition of exogenous PGE2 reversed the enhanced DC-recruitment effect of both inhibitors (Figure S6). The data confirm that the restored NK–DC crosstalk is driven by PGE2 depletion per se, rather than off-target effects of celecoxib.

disp-quote.p: (1) Senescence heterogeneity is not addressed in the current study. Given growing awareness that senescent cells are not a uniform population, a brief discussion acknowledging this point would be appropriate.

body.p: We have added a paragraph to the Discussion acknowledging that senescent cells constitute a highly heterogeneous population, and that senescence-inducer-dependent variability should be systematically mapped in future platform optimizations.

disp-quote.p: (2) Terminology alternates between "live vaccine" and "whole tumor cell vaccine"; consistent terminology would improve clarity.

body.p: Thank you for pointing this out. In the revised manuscript, we have unified the terminology, consistently referring to the platform as a “senescent tumor cell (STC)-based live vaccine”.

disp-quote.p: (3) The discussion could be strengthened by clearly addressing translational considerations such as autologous versus allogeneic STCs, scalability, and regulatory challenges associated with live senescent cells.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. We have expanded the Discussion to address key translational aspects. Specifically, we contrasted the personalized antigen fidelity of autologous cells with the scalability and biobanking advantages of allogeneic platforms. We also delineated the regulatory and manufacturing hurdles associated with live senescent cells, focusing on the verification of irreversible arrest, SASP management, and GMP standardization.
